working_title: Why turning your thermostat higher won't heat the room faster

fact_sources.claim: A room thermostat senses air temperature, calls for heat below the setting, and stops that call at the setting. Raising the setting does not speed up heating.

beats.narration: Higher won't heat this room faster.
beats.visible_action: Thermostat dial jumps from 22 to 30 degrees while the cold room stays blue

beats.narration: The thermostat is a switch, not a gas pedal.
beats.visible_action: Transparent thermostat reveals a single contact closing, with no speed control

beats.narration: It measures the air. Right now, it's eighteen degrees.
beats.visible_action: Air particles drift through a sensor; measured temperature reads 18

beats.narration: You ask for twenty-two. It calls the boiler for heat.
beats.visible_action: Setpoint becomes 22; a signal travels to the boiler control

beats.narration: The boiler heats water, which flows through the radiator.
beats.visible_action: Boiler burner lights; orange water moves through pipes into radiator

beats.narration: Warm air spreads through the room as the temperature climbs.
beats.visible_action: Heat rises from radiator and room counter advances from 18 to 21

beats.narration: At twenty-two, the thermostat stops asking for heat.
beats.visible_action: Room counter reaches 22; thermostat contact opens; heat call stops

beats.narration: Thirty degrees only makes it run longer, not faster.
beats.visible_action: Side-by-side setpoints 22 and 30 share the same heating rate; the 30 line continues longer

loop_resolution: The 30 degree dial at the end matches the first frame's mistaken adjustment.
